questions.q: Why does prompt injection work against an LLM in a way that's distinct from classic SQL injection?
options: It doesn't — prompt injection is just SQL injection renamed for a new technology
Because the model has no hard boundary between content it's told to process and instructions it's told to follow, so attacker-supplied text can be read as a command
Because LLMs store all user input directly in a relational database without escaping
Because prompt injection only works when the model is run without any API authentication
questions.explain: SQL injection tricks a database engine into treating data as code via an escaping failure. Prompt injection works because the model was never given a code/data boundary at all — it reads instructions and content as the same kind of material.

questions.q: What does it mean that an LLM's output is 'non-deterministic,' and why does that matter for security testing?
options: It means the model always produces the exact same output for the exact same input, which makes testing easier
It means the model only runs on nondeterministic hardware like GPUs, which is irrelevant to security
It means the same prompt can produce different output on different runs, so passing a test once doesn't guarantee it keeps passing, and keyword blocklists can be bypassed by rephrasing
It means the model's weights change automatically every time it answers a question
questions.explain: LLMs sample from a probability distribution over outputs. That breaks the deterministic-testing assumption security teams rely on and makes fixed keyword/content filters easy to bypass by rephrasing.

questions.q: Why do training data and model weights count as new security assets that didn't exist in traditional application security?
options: Because a model can memorize and reproduce fragments of its training data, and because weights are both valuable IP and a target for attacks that need white-box access
Because training data and model weights are always encrypted by default in every AI framework
Because they are never accessed by anyone other than the original model vendor
Because they only matter for models trained entirely on public, non-sensitive data
questions.explain: Memorized training data can leak back out through normal model use, and stolen or exposed weights represent stolen IP and enable offline attacks like crafting adversarial inputs or extracting training data.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the relationship between AI security and traditional security disciplines like API security and access control?
options: AI security replaces those disciplines entirely, since LLMs don't use APIs or run behind authentication
AI security has no relationship to those disciplines and should be handled by a completely separate, unrelated team with no shared practices
Traditional security disciplines are obsolete once an AI feature is added to a product
AI security is additive — it sits on top of those still-necessary disciplines as a new layer the model's reasoning over untrusted input adds
questions.explain: LLM features still run behind APIs that need authentication and rate-limiting, and still touch data that needs classification and protection. AI security adds a new layer on top of those fundamentals rather than retiring them.

questions.q: Why can't a traditional input-validation approach (enumerate valid input, reject everything else) fully contain prompt injection risk?
options: Because input validation is impossible to implement in any programming language used for AI
Because prompt injection attacks are always submitted through SQL queries instead of text prompts
Because the LLM reads natural language as a command channel rather than parsing it against a fixed grammar, so the space of possible attacker phrasing is effectively unbounded
Because traditional input validation only works on image files, not text
questions.explain: A traditional app parses input against rules you defined, so you can enumerate what's valid. An LLM reads everything in its context as potential instruction, and there's no fixed grammar to validate against — the attack surface is the space of everything that can be phrased.
